---
title: "What else looks like age? Linkage, inbreeding, drift, dropout, gene flow and selection"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.2,
                      dpi = 110, out.width = "100%", echo = FALSE)
library(hybridclock)
red <- "#E8202A"; blue <- "#2B55D5"; purple <- "#9B2FC9"; grey <- "#BDBDBD"
gold <- "#E6A817"; dark <- "#4D4D4D"

# one individual as a large circle holding two allele dots
genotype_circle <- function(x, y, a1, a2, r = 0.38, faded = c(FALSE, FALSE)) {
  symbols(x, y, circles = r, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE, fg = "grey55", lwd = 1.3)
  for (k in 1:2) {
    col <- c(a1, a2)[k]; dx <- c(-0.15, 0.15)[k]
    if (faded[k]) symbols(x + dx, y, circles = 0.11, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE, fg = col, lwd = 1.5, lty = 2)
    else symbols(x + dx, y, circles = 0.11, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE, bg = col, fg = col)
  }
}

# a row of individuals; g = genotypes coded 0/1/2 (copies of the species-2 allele)
genotype_row <- function(g, y, label, cols = c(red, blue)) {
  text(-0.2, y, label, adj = 1, cex = 0.9)
  for (i in seq_along(g)) {
    a <- if (g[i] == 0) cols[c(1, 1)] else if (g[i] == 2) cols[c(2, 2)] else cols
    genotype_circle(i, y, a[1], a[2])
  }
}

blank <- function(xlim, ylim) {
  par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", asp = 1)
}

# the hybrid triangle with points colored by group
triangle <- function(S, H, group, cols, main = "", legend_pos = "topright", cex = 1) {
  par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Hybrid index (S)",
       ylab = "Interspecies heterozygosity (H)", main = main, las = 1, cex.main = 1)
  lines(c(0, 0.5, 1), c(0, 1, 0), col = "grey70")
  s <- seq(0, 1, 0.01); lines(s, 2 * s * (1 - s), col = "grey70", lty = 2)
  for (g in names(cols)) points(S[group == g], H[group == g], pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(cols[[g]], 0.6), cex = cex)
  legend(legend_pos, names(cols), col = unlist(cols), pch = 16, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
}

# painted chromosomes: one row per individual, genotypes along a map
paint <- function(G, map, rows, main = "", marks = NULL, y0 = 0) {
  chroms <- sort(unique(map$chromosome))
  len <- tapply(map$position, map$chromosome, max)
  gap <- 0.06 * sum(len); xs <- c(0, cumsum(len + gap))[seq_along(chroms)]
  for (k in seq_along(rows)) {
    y <- y0 - k
    for (j in seq_along(chroms)) {
      m <- which(map$chromosome == chroms[j]); p <- map$position[m]
      edges <- c(0, (p[-1] + p[-length(p)]) / 2, len[j])
      col <- c(red, purple, blue)[G[rows[k], m] + 1]
      rect(xs[j] + edges[-length(edges)], y - 0.32, xs[j] + edges[-1], y + 0.32, col = col, border = NA)
      rect(xs[j], y - 0.32, xs[j] + len[j], y + 0.32, border = "grey40")
    }
  }
  if (!is.null(marks)) for (j in seq_along(chroms)) {
    mm <- marks[marks$chromosome == chroms[j], ]
    points(xs[j] + mm$position, rep(y0 - 0.25, nrow(mm)), pch = 8, cex = 0.7, col = dark)
  }
  text(xs + len / 2, y0 - length(rows) - 0.9, paste("chromosome", chroms), cex = 0.8, col = "grey30")
  if (nzchar(main)) text(sum(len + gap) / 2, y0 + 0.55, main, cex = 0.95, font = 2)
}
```

hybridclock reads the age of a hybrid population from the hybrid index
(*S*, the share of alleles from species 2) and interspecies heterozygosity
(*H*, the share of markers with one allele from each species) of its
individuals, and from how those vary across individuals and markers. Several
other processes change the same patterns without any change in age. This
article shows what each one does, why it can be mistaken for age, and how
hybridclock keeps it apart. The figures are drawn from the package's own
simulator, except for selection, which is illustrated.

## The starting point: why later generations look alike

Each large circle below is one individual at one diagnostic marker, and the
two dots inside are its two alleles: red from species 1, blue from species 2.
F1s carry one allele from each species. In F2s, a quarter are red-red, half
red-blue and a quarter blue-blue. The F3 generation, and every later
generation of a randomly mating swarm, has the same expected mix, so a
single marker in a single individual cannot tell an F2 from an F8.

```{r generations, fig.height = 3.3}
set.seed(4)
blank(c(-1.6, 10.5), c(0.4, 5.6))
genotype_row(rep(0, 10), 5, "species 1")
genotype_row(rep(2, 10), 4, "species 2")
genotype_row(rep(1, 10), 3, "F1")
genotype_row(c(0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 1), 2, "F2")
genotype_row(c(1, 2, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0), 1, "F3 and later")
```

Across many markers, an individual's *S* and *H* are averages of these
one-marker pictures. What changes with age is subtler: how genotypes are
arranged along chromosomes, how unevenly ancestry is spread across markers,
and how often individuals look like recent crosses. The processes below
change those same patterns.

## Linkage

Markers on the same chromosome are inherited together until recombination
separates them. In the first hybrid generations the blocks of each species'
ancestry are long; every generation of recombination cuts them shorter.
Below, five individuals from the second hybrid generation (top) and the eighth
(bottom) of the same closed population are painted along three chromosomes:
red where both copies come from species 1, blue where both come from species
2, and purple where the individual is heterozygous. Asterisks mark a typical
panel of 30 markers.

```{r linkage-paint, fig.height = 5.2}
set.seed(11)
map <- random_map(1200, chromosomes = 3, length_cM = 300)
sim <- simulate_hybrid_zone(generations = 8, breeders = 80, founders = "F1", n_markers = 1200,
                            map = map, sample_at = c(1, 8), seed = 11)
smp <- attr(sim, "samples")
panel <- map[sort(sample.int(nrow(map), 30)), ]
par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(NA, xlim = c(-5, 330), ylim = c(-15.5, 1), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
paint(smp[["1"]]$genotypes, map, rows = 1:5, main = "Second hybrid generation (F2)", marks = panel, y0 = 0)
paint(smp[["8"]]$genotypes, map, rows = 1:5, main = "Eighth hybrid generation", marks = panel, y0 = -7.5)
legend("bottom", c("species 1 / species 1", "heterozygous", "species 2 / species 2", "marker"),
       fill = c(red, purple, blue, NA), border = NA, pch = c(NA, NA, NA, 8), col = c(NA, NA, NA, dark),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8, horiz = TRUE)
```

Within one individual, markers that sit in the same long block all report
the same ancestry, so they repeat one piece of information rather than adding
new ones. An individual's *S* and *H* are averages over its markers, and with
long blocks those averages rest on only a few independent pieces. Averages of
a few pieces vary more than averages of many, so F2s typed at linked markers
differ from one another much more than F2s typed at unlinked markers: one may
happen to carry mostly species-2 blocks, another mostly species-1 blocks. The
triangle shows F2 families typed at 30 markers, either unlinked or on three
short chromosomes.

```{r linkage-triangle, fig.height = 4.6, fig.width = 6.5, out.width = "75%", fig.align = "center"}
f2 <- function(map, seed) {
  s <- simulate_hybrid_zone(generations = 1, breeders = 30, founders = "F1", n_markers = 30,
                            sample_size = 60, map = map, sample_at = 1, seed = seed)
  attr(s, "samples")[["1"]]
}
a <- f2(NULL, 1); b <- f2(random_map(30, 3, 150), 1)
triangle(c(a$S, b$S), c(a$H, b$H), rep(c("F2, unlinked markers", "F2, linked markers"), each = 60),
         list("F2, unlinked markers" = red, "F2, linked markers" = purple))
```

A spread like this is not what a single F2 family looks like when markers
are assumed to be independent. It looks like a mix of hybrid classes: some
individuals near the F1 corner, others near the backcrosses or below the
dashed curve, where later generations fall. Classified one at a time on the
assumption that markers are independent, only about 40% of these F2s are
called F2, and a fifth are called later-generation hybrids:

```{r linkage-classes, fig.height = 3.6, fig.width = 7, out.width = "85%", fig.align = "center"}
calls <- function(map_fun, eff) unlist(lapply(1:20, function(i) {
  x <- f2(map_fun(), i)
  as.character(classify_hybrids(data.frame(S = x$S, H = x$H, n_markers = 30), effective_markers = eff)$class)
}))
grp <- function(v) {
  v <- ifelse(v == "F2", "F2", ifelse(v == "later", "later", ifelse(grepl("^BC", v), "backcross", "other")))
  100 * prop.table(table(factor(v, levels = c("F2", "backcross", "later", "other"))))
}
tab <- cbind("unlinked\nmarkers" = grp(calls(function() NULL, NULL)),
             "linked\nmarkers" = grp(calls(function() random_map(30, 3, 150), NULL)),
             "linked, with\neffective_markers" = grp(calls(function() random_map(30, 3, 150), effective_markers(3, 150))))
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 9), xpd = TRUE)
barplot(tab, col = c(purple, gold, blue, grey), border = NA, las = 1, ylab = "Percent of true F2s",
        cex.names = 0.85)
legend("right", inset = c(-0.32, 0), rev(rownames(tab)), fill = rev(c(purple, gold, blue, grey)),
       border = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.85, title = "Called")
```

So an F2 family typed at linked markers can be read as a more mixed, more
advanced population than it is.

**How hybridclock handles it.** The simulated reference includes linkage:
either the real genetic map (`map`, with `map_scale` for uncertainty in its
length) or a range of chromosome numbers and map lengths, so clustered
markers in the data are compared with simulations that cluster the same way.
For individual classes, `effective_markers()` tells the classifier how many
independent markers a linked panel is worth, which removes the false
"later" calls (right-hand bar above); with so few independent markers, the
remaining classes stay uncertain, which is why the population clock relies on
simulations that include linkage. With a map, the clock also counts how often
an individual's genotype switches between neighboring markers. Those switches mark the boundaries between
ancestry blocks, and they become more common with every generation:

```{r switches, fig.height = 3.6, fig.width = 6.5, out.width = "75%", fig.align = "center"}
sw <- simulate_hybrid_zone(generations = 20, breeders = 200, founders = "F1", n_markers = 1200,
                           map = map, junctions = TRUE, seed = 3)
par(mar = c(4, 5.5, 1, 1))
plot(sw$generation, sw$switch_rate, type = "b", pch = 16, col = purple, las = 1,
     xlab = "Hybrid generation", ylab = "Ancestry switches\nper marker interval")
```

## Inbreeding

Inbreeding (mating between relatives, for example in small breeding groups)
removes heterozygotes. Below, the top two rows show a diagnostic marker in a
young, inbred population and in an older population that mates at random:
both have fewer heterozygotes than an F2. The bottom two rows show a marker
that is polymorphic within both species (gold and grey alleles, with nothing
to do with hybrid ancestry). There the two populations differ: only the
inbred one is missing heterozygotes.

```{r inbreeding-beads, fig.height = 3.4}
blank(c(-3.2, 10.5), c(0.4, 4.8))
text(-3.2, 4.6, "diagnostic marker", adj = 0, cex = 0.85, font = 3)
genotype_row(c(0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 0, 1, 2, 2, 0), 4, "young, inbred")
genotype_row(c(0, 1, 0, 2, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0), 3, "older, random mating")
text(-3.2, 2.6, "marker variable within species", adj = 0, cex = 0.85, font = 3)
genotype_row(c(0, 0, 2, 2, 0, 2, 0, 0, 2, 1), 2, "young, inbred", cols = c(gold, grey))
genotype_row(c(1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1), 1, "older, random mating", cols = c(gold, grey))
```

Lower heterozygosity at diagnostic markers is a sign of age, so inbreeding
alone can make a young population look old. The simulations below compare
populations at the fifth hybrid generation, bred in three small groups with
frequent sibling mating, against populations of 60 breeders that have mated
at random for thirty generations. At the diagnostic markers they look alike:
both have about 20% fewer heterozygotes than random mating at their ancestry
would give (left). Only the inbred populations are also missing heterozygotes
at markers that vary within species (right, the inbreeding coefficient at
those markers).

```{r inbreeding-sims, fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(1)
shared <- runif(150, 0.2, 0.8)
run <- function(g, n, sib, pools, seed) simulate_hybrid_zone(generations = g, breeders = n,
  sib_mating = sib, pools = pools, pool_crossing = 0.02, founders = "F1", n_markers = 300,
  shared_freq = shared, sample_size = 30, seed = seed)[g, c("het_floor_ratio", "shared_fis")]
inb <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:25, function(i) run(5, 30, 0.8, 3, i)))
old <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:25, function(i) run(30, 60, 0, 1, 100 + i)))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 1.5, 1))
boxplot(list("5th generation,\ninbred" = inb$het_floor_ratio, "30th generation,\nrandom mating" = old$het_floor_ratio),
        col = c(gold, purple), las = 1, ylab = "Observed / expected H", main = "Diagnostic markers", cex.main = 0.95)
boxplot(list("5th generation,\ninbred" = inb$shared_fis, "30th generation,\nrandom mating" = old$shared_fis),
        col = c(gold, purple), las = 1, ylab = "Inbreeding coefficient", main = "Markers variable within species",
        cex.main = 0.95)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
```

**How hybridclock handles it.** Markers that vary within both species
(`shared_loci()`) give a separate measure of inbreeding and linkage
disequilibrium, and the simulated reference includes sibling mating and
separate breeding pools (`sib_mating`, `pools`). The clock learns to read
age from the diagnostic markers while accounting for inbreeding measured at
the shared ones.

## Drift

Each generation, a breeding population passes on a random sample of its
alleles, like drawing beads from a jar. At each marker, the share of
species-2 ancestry wanders away from the population average, and the
smaller the population, the faster it wanders. Below, each jar is one marker,
and its 20 beads show the share of species-2 ancestry (blue) at that marker
in the population.

```{r drift-jars, fig.height = 3.2}
jar_row <- function(G, y, label) {
  text(-0.6, y + 0.9, label, adj = 0, cex = 0.85, font = 3)
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(G))) {
    x0 <- (j - 1) * 2.2
    rect(x0, y - 1.1, x0 + 1.8, y + 0.6, border = "grey45", lwd = 1.3)
    n2 <- round(20 * mean(G[, j]) / 2)
    al <- rep(c(0, 1), c(20 - n2, n2))
    for (k in seq_along(al)) {
      cx <- x0 + 0.25 + ((k - 1) %% 4) * 0.43; cy <- y - 0.9 + ((k - 1) %/% 4) * 0.3
      symbols(cx, cy, circles = 0.13, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE, bg = c(red, blue)[al[k] + 1], fg = NA)
    }
  }
}
pick <- function(n, g, seed) {
  s <- simulate_hybrid_zone(generations = g, breeders = n, founders = "F1", n_markers = 400,
                            sample_size = 200, sample_at = g, seed = seed)
  attr(s, "samples")[[as.character(g)]]$genotypes
}
G_large <- pick(500, 15, 2); G_small <- pick(20, 15, 2)
blank(c(-0.8, 17.5), c(-4.6, 3.6))
jar_row(G_large[, 1:8], 2, "large population (500 breeders), fifteenth generation")
jar_row(G_small[, 1:8], -2, "small population (20 breeders), fifteenth generation")
```

Drift acts on allele frequencies. In a population founded by F1s, every
diagnostic marker starts with half its alleles from each species. As the
share at each marker wanders, two things happen at once:

- **at each marker, the alleles become more alike.** As the share moves
  toward 0 or 1, more and more individuals carry the same species' allele
  there, so individuals also become more alike;
- **across markers, the shares become more different.** Some markers end up
  mostly species 1 and others mostly species 2, so ancestry becomes uneven
  along the genome.

These are the same process seen two ways. hybridclock measures the second
as the variance of the species-2 share across markers, divided by its
largest possible value. It runs from 0, when every marker has the same
share, to 1, when every marker is fixed for one species or the other (like
*F*~ST~, with markers in place of populations). On the left below are the
shares at all 400 markers in the two populations above; on the right is the
measure over 30 generations at three breeding sizes:

```{r drift-lines, fig.height = 3.8}
d <- lapply(c(20, 100, 500), function(n) {
  r <- lapply(1:8, function(i) simulate_hybrid_zone(generations = 30, breeders = n, founders = "F1",
                                                    n_markers = 200, sample_size = 60, seed = i))
  Reduce(`+`, lapply(r, `[`, c("generation", "marker_spread"))) / 8
})
cols <- c(gold, "#8C8C8C", dark)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 5, 1.5, 1))
br <- seq(0, 1, 0.05)
h_large <- hist(colMeans(G_large) / 2, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)
h_small <- hist(colMeans(G_small) / 2, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, max(h_large$counts, h_small$counts)), las = 1,
     xlab = "Share of species-2 alleles at a marker", ylab = "Markers",
     main = "Fifteenth generation", cex.main = 0.95)
rect(br[-length(br)], 0, br[-1], h_large$counts, col = adjustcolor(dark, 0.6), border = "white")
rect(br[-length(br)], 0, br[-1], h_small$counts, col = adjustcolor(gold, 0.7), border = "white")
legend("topright", c("500 breeders", "20 breeders"), fill = c(adjustcolor(dark, 0.6), adjustcolor(gold, 0.7)),
       border = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 30), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(d, `[[`, "marker_spread"))), las = 1,
     xlab = "Hybrid generation", ylab = "", main = "Uneven ancestry across markers", cex.main = 0.95)
title(ylab = "Variance of the share (0 to 1)", line = 3.5)
for (k in 1:3) lines(d[[k]]$generation, d[[k]]$marker_spread, col = cols[k], lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", paste(c(20, 100, 500), "breeders"), col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

Ancestry becomes uneven with time, and in a closed population its pace
depends on the breeding size. A small population reaches in a few
generations the unevenness that a large one reaches only after many, so
time and breeding size trade off: a small population can look as old as a
much older large one.

Separate populations drift independently, so the same marker can end up
mostly species 1 in one population and mostly species 2 in another, and
the populations grow apart. hybridclock dates each population on its own and
does not use that divergence.

Drift is also tied to linkage and inbreeding. In a small population, drift
creates associations between markers even on different chromosomes (linkage
disequilibrium), and mating among relatives becomes unavoidable, so drift,
linkage disequilibrium and inbreeding grow together. Linkage disequilibrium
from drift pushes the same way as linkage on a chromosome: markers that are
inherited together make individuals differ more. In the simulations, though,
the alleles becoming more alike at each marker outweigh it, and individuals
still become more alike as the population drifts. hybridclock measures
linkage disequilibrium and inbreeding at markers that vary within species,
and its simulations combine breeding size, mating among relatives and the
map, so the clock sees these processes together rather than one at a time.

**How hybridclock handles it.** In a closed population, after the first few
generations drift is the main clock. The reference draws the breeding size from a range (`breeders`), so
the estimate allows for any size in that range. Give the widest range that
is plausible: a range that misses the true size gives precise but wrong
ages, while a generous one only widens the interval.

## Heterozygote dropout

With low sequencing depth or allele-specific failure, one allele of a
heterozygote can go undetected, and the individual is called homozygous
(dashed dot below). Missing heterozygotes look like the loss of
heterozygosity that comes with age, so individuals slide down the triangle.

```{r dropout-beads, fig.height = 1.6}
blank(c(-2.6, 10.5), c(0.4, 1.6))
text(-0.2, 1, "heterozygotes\n(dashed: allele missed)", adj = 1, cex = 0.8)
for (i in 1:10) genotype_circle(i, 1, red, blue, faded = c(FALSE, i %in% c(3, 7)))
```

```{r dropout-triangle, fig.height = 4.6, fig.width = 6.5, out.width = "75%", fig.align = "center"}
obs <- function(dr) attr(simulate_hybrid_zone(generations = 3, breeders = 100, n_markers = 300,
                                              sample_size = 60, het_dropout = dr, sample_at = 3, seed = 21),
                         "samples")[["3"]]
o0 <- obs(0); o1 <- obs(0.25)
triangle(c(o0$S, o1$S), c(o0$H, o1$H), rep(c("no dropout", "25% of heterozygotes missed"), each = 60),
         list("no dropout" = purple, "25% of heterozygotes missed" = gold))
```

**How hybridclock handles it.** The reference simulates dropout over a range
(`het_dropout`), and the classifier behind the class shares is told the
dropout rate through `class_settings(het_dropout = ...)`, so the simulated and
the real samples are read the same way. The bettongs in the
[full tutorial](tutorial.html) are an example.

## Continuing gene flow

When pure individuals of one species keep arriving, they mate with hybrids
and start new, short pedigree lines. Hybrid age then stops growing and
levels off, however long the species have been in contact:

```{r gene-flow, fig.height = 3.8, fig.width = 6.5, out.width = "75%", fig.align = "center"}
gf <- lapply(c(0, 0.02, 0.05), function(r)
  simulate_hybrid_zone(generations = 30, breeders = 200, start_mix = 0.5, arrivals = c(r, 0),
                       n_markers = 300, sample_size = 40, seed = 8))
par(mar = c(4, 5.5, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 30), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(gf, `[[`, "hybrid_age_both"), na.rm = TRUE)),
     las = 1, xlab = "Generations since contact", ylab = "Hybrid age")
for (k in 1:3) lines(gf[[k]]$generation, gf[[k]]$hybrid_age_both, col = cols[k], lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("closed", "2% new arrivals per generation", "5% new arrivals per generation"),
       col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

This is not an error: hybrid age measures the pedigrees of the hybrids, not
the time since contact. But it means that a young-looking population may
have been in contact for a long time.

**How hybridclock handles it.** The reference includes arrivals of either
species, at constant rates or rates that stop or start partway, and the
package also reports the hybrid age of the rarer species' lines and the
probability that pure individuals are still arriving. With continuing gene
flow, hybrid age is a lower bound on the time since contact.

## Selection

Selection against one species' ancestry in parts of the genome removes that
ancestry from those regions faster than drift would. The painting below
illustrates this (it is a drawing, not a simulation): the same individuals as
in the linkage section, with species-2 ancestry purged from most of
chromosome 2.

```{r selection-paint, fig.height = 4.6}
G8 <- smp[["8"]]$genotypes[1:5, seq_len(nrow(map))]
Gsel <- G8
on2 <- which(map$chromosome == 2 & map$position > 15 & map$position < 85)
Gsel[, on2] <- pmax(0L, Gsel[, on2] - 1L)
par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(NA, xlim = c(-5, 330), ylim = c(-14, 1), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
paint(G8, map, rows = 1:5, main = "Eighth generation, no selection", y0 = 0)
paint(Gsel, map, rows = 1:5, main = "Illustration: species-2 ancestry selected against on chromosome 2", y0 = -7.5)
```

Regions under selection carry less heterozygosity and more uneven ancestry
than the rest of the genome, which is what drift and age produce too. In
experimental sunflower hybrids under strong selection, estimates ran ahead of
the true number of generations for several generations.

**How hybridclock handles it.** It doesn't: the simulations assume neutral
markers. Leaving out the most differentiated markers did not help in the
sunflowers, because the selected blocks covered several whole chromosomes.
Where strong selection is suspected, estimates may be too old.

## Summary

| Process | How it can look like age | What hybridclock does |
|---|---|---|
| Linkage | linked markers make an F2 family look like a mix of hybrid classes | simulates the map, or a range of maps; `effective_markers()` for classes; counts ancestry switches with a real map |
| Inbreeding | fewer heterozygotes at diagnostic markers | measures inbreeding at shared loci; simulates sibling mating and breeding pools |
| Drift | uneven ancestry across markers builds up faster in small populations | draws the breeding size from a range |
| Heterozygote dropout | missed heterozygotes lower *H* | simulates dropout; the classifier is told the rate |
| Continuing gene flow | hybrid age levels off | simulates arrivals; reports the rarer species' age and the probability of arrivals |
| Selection | purged regions look like drift | not modeled: a stated limitation |

The settings for each are described in the
[getting-started vignette](../articles/hybridclock.html), and the
[full tutorial](tutorial.html) applies them to five real datasets.
